Baboons run amok

By: Liz Fish | Commission

Proposal


Show:

Unique Selling Point:
There baboons have literally moved into town, taking over, and nobody is taking responsibility and the level of trauma of residents is falling on deaf ears, never mind the level of damage to property. A few statistics from Kommetjie - 55% of residents have DAILY encounters with baboons; 70% have had damage to their property; 85% have had baboons in their homes; 35% keep their windows permanently closed; and 11 % have had to have pets euthanased.

Baboons are holding residents hostage in their own homes in Kommetjie and Simon’s Town. They are no longer afraid of people. They used to be frightened of men but they have become so habituated that if confronted they just bare their teeth and rise up in attack stance.
Children are so traumatised that they won’t play in their own gardens. They are not safe at home or school. The baboons recently walked into a preschool and grabbed the food from the hands of a terrified 3-year-old, a carefree confident child now clings to her mother’s legs.
A large male baboon slipped into a home and entered the bedroom where a dog was asleep. The startled dog awoke and was ripped apart. Its eye torn out, ear ripped off and scalped. The vet had no alternative but to euthanase it. A dog let out to relieve itself in the rain after its owner had checked the baboon alert group was attacked so badly, it also had to be euthanased. A child with severe autism’s companion labrador came between a child and a baboon when it entered their home; both child and dog are now severely traumatised


Summary:
For the last 3 years, the once internationally recognised urban wildlife baboon management programme has broken down after a massive social media campaign waged by baboon activists after the Kataza saga. The situation came to a head in Kommetjie last Sunday when residents held a peaceful protest outside a burned-out building in the main street of Kommetjie.
The baboons come down from the mountain every night and are escorted into town by a self-appointed baboon monitor, Briton Pauline Sudders. Her concern is that they don’t get run over - but she doesn’t stop there. She shouts at children skateboarding that they must keep quiet because the baboons want to sleep and confronts people carrying any kind of defence against being attacked.
Matters have been brewing since the Kataza saga 3 years ago where residents protested the relocation of a male baboon from Kommetjie to Constantia, which the baboon activists saw as him being removed from his family. Activist Jenni Trethowan escorted him back over the mountain, but on hisd return, Kataza rejected his so-called “family” and headed out again. He was relocated to Limpopo amid a media storm, and later released into an area where farmers boast of having shot over 200 baboons – there is a good chance Kataza has also been shot.
Kataza was a turning point for the City of Cape Town because the social media backlash was so extreme. This activist media campaign called on international tourists to boycott Cape Town because “we kill baboons”. The city could ill afford to lose any more tourism after the Covid-19 pandemic.
Internationally recognised wildlife academic and baboon specialist, Dr Justin O Riain, was labelled “Dr Death” and a deep fake video circulated of him “doing vivisections”. Complaints were lodged on a daily basis to his employers, UCT. He was investigated numerous times and eventually asked to stop his research because the media campaign was so vicious. It nearly ended his career. He received repeat death threats to both himself and his family. The City stopped implementing the scientific protocols on how to deal with wildlife on the urban edge - a world-recognised programme that had worked for over 10 years. Fake science and the emotive media campaign were too much for the authorities.
Now when residents are being attacked in their own homes, the baboon activists stand outside and say “I am filming you - don’t hurt the baboons”, and offer no help. This is a voice note from a mother whose entire week’s food was destroyed, her 10-year-old trapped under the stairs. For three days running, the same baboon attacked her home. One evening her 6 foot tall, 19-year-old champion windsurfer son tried to hold the door closed in the face of an aggressive male baboon - he lost the tussle and the baboon got in, trapping them in the bedroom. People fear defending themselves because their activist neighbours threaten to burn their homes down
The three responsible authorities - SANparks, CapeNature and the City of Cape Town - have for decades tossed this hot potato back and forth, all claiming they either don’t have jurisdiction or funding. Finally, in 2023 then Environment Minister Barbara Creecey interceded and appointed a Joint task Team. SANParks agreed to put R8-million into strategic electrified baboon fences. CapeNature put in R2-million but don’t have budget for operational costs; and the COCT are cancelling the rangers’ contract at the end of September. The fences are useless without rangers.

Script:


"I got into a bit of a shock, I feel like vomiting all the time. I mean, I have never ever felt like that with the baboons before. But it was extremely aggressive, both of them…..”
VO: A voice note from a resident of a coastal community outside Cape Town... moments after encountering baboons in her home
Margie “ I was screaming and screaming and trying to trying to hit them apart.
Michael:. The baboons have a lot of rights. I have no rights at all
Belinda “they look at you and they walk straight past you into the kitchen.
VO: A longstanding suburban conflict between wild animals - and humans.
Peter: there is a very fine line between admiring a baboon, and treating them as though they were your sort of public pets.
VO: And - it’s reaching breaking point.
Pauline: They are not dangerous
breather
UPSOUND of Kommetjie conflict people shouting
VO: Few issues divide coastal communities more than baboons - as this standoff in Kommetjie, on the Cape Peninsula early last month shows.
upsound from standoff
VO: About 40 baboons had spent most of the winter sleeping in town - raiding the village in the day - and some residents- had had enough
Upsound standoff
VO: As their natural habitats shrink, baboons are becoming increasingly habituated in urban spaces across the Peninsula, like Kommetjie and Simonstown.
Margie “By this stage the baboon was here passing me , it came through here, Lila was on the chair over there and she spotted it
VO: Kommetjie resident Margret Kennedy, has vivid memories of a serious encounter with baboons. She was inside her house at the time - and had left the front door open. A local WhatsApp alert group indicated there were no baboons in the vicinity."
Margie “there was just blood everywhere and I ran next door to get Wayne
Wayne “The baboon got me in my hand. But then it would go back to Lila and continually, like, shredding her.
VO: Baboons had got into her home, and were attacking her dog. The Pitbull lost an eye - and had an ear ripped off… and was later euthanized.
Margie: I was told on that day that it was an isolated incident and nothing like that had ever happened before. 00:11:28:05 and I was also blamed for leaving my front door open
VO: But it wasn’t isolated - incidents like this have been escalating. In some areas, like central Simonstown, baboons have taken up permanent residence.
LINK “Only 25% of the baboons actually go back into the mountains at night which means there are generations and generations of baboon babies that only know city living , they occupy abandoned buildings, they forage, they eat the stuff in the rubbish , they have become part of Simonstown
VO: Peter Willis has been living in Simonstown for 31 years.
Govan: Have baboons always been a problem here?
Peter: No…….In the mid 2000, they started coming down and it was it got pretty bad
VO: In 2010 - the City of Cape Town intervened, developing a baboon management and monitoring protocol, and for 10 years, the baboons stayed largely in the mountains
Peter “And then we hit Covid and the troops started realizing they could move in places that they hadn't previously.
VO: Residents were working from home; some were feeding the baboons.
They saw firsthand how the monitors controversially drove the animals out with paintball guns, relocated them, and occasionally euthanized them.
It led to accusations of cruelty and ineptitude against City officials, some of whom - had their tyres slashed or were threatened.
Respected Behaviour Ecologist, Professor Justin O Riain, wasn’t spared: He and his family were threatened - and his job put at risk.
Justin: And that was probably the most difficult lesson I learned was that facts can't beat Facebook.
VO: Amid the public mud-slinging, the baboon management program lost funding - and slowly became ineffectual.
Justin: I think they should have had the backbone to stand up and say, well, that's your opinion, … we're carrying on like this because it's the right thing to do. It's rational, it's supported by science and communities, and baboons are benefiting
VO: In the vacuum, - the baboons moved in.
LINK “There are two baboons in this rubbish bin right now ….1.47 this is why the baboons are in such bad shape. …………… they eating out of rubbish bins and when they cant find anything here, they go into people’s homes
Breather
Polly Clip “. This was locked. Unfortunately, those two bottom ones weren't. And .. She took out the whole of this window
VO: Polly Saul lives alone - and no longer sits outside in her garden.
Polly” I was shocked and shattered because everything was closed and locked., and a avo rolled across the counter. So it leapt to follow the other, and I think it thought assumed I was going to take its purchase, and it just leaned over to make sure I didn't. And I think in the process it caught my hand,
VO: Baboons carry many diseases, and leave behind huge amounts of faeces.
Polly needed a tetanus shot.
Polly Clip “And their skills are improving massively and we are helpless.
VO: Baboons are actively breaking in - chewing through wooden window frames
and breaking burglar bars
and trapping dogs inside homes.
Breath/beat
VO: In August, filmmaker, Micheal Donnely, returned to a house turned upside down by 16 baboons.
Michael “I come upstairs and at this stage I have no idea how these guys have got in… there is poos all over the steps all over the walls and everywhere here
“They got in here and broke the latch
Govan “All this gear, did the gear get damaged
A lot- there was a camera that they poop in, they threw it out the window, there a 35 mm lens and 1.2 and I have no idea where it is
“I think we are looking at R250 000 maybe R300 000 seriously
Michael:. The baboons have a lot of rights. I feel that I have no rights in this thing that nobody's listening to what is happening here? Everyone is pretending it's a sort of a non-event
VO: Since June 2022 SANParks, Cape Nature, and the City, collectively called the JTT, have been formulating an urban baboon strategic management plan.
But the process has been marred by political infighting and budget disagreements.
Now - the City has terminated what’s left of the existing baboon monitoring program.
Breather
LINK “Residents feel the authorities are missing in action and their desperate pleas for help disappear into the void
VO: Animal activists like Pauline Suddards - are trying to fill the gap.
Pauline: when the baboons move across the road. And then I have a flag just to warn traffic because the baboons' fur is the same colour as the tarmac. And to also keep them safe so that nobody interferes with them before they go to roost.
Govan: Is that a self-appointed function?
Pauline: Um, when you say self-appointed, if I'm there doing traffic control, um, I just make sure that they, you know, they stay away from danger really
VO: Like many in these areas, Pauline believes people who choose to live here - should adapt to the baboons.
Pauline: You know, you need to embrace what comes with Kommetjie. All the wildlife, the otters, the baboons, everything that's here.
Justin: I think suggesting to people that they should learn to live with baboons in a suburb is is a very bad idea. And our data is clear on this, that if baboons spend time in urban areas, they will suffer from all manner of injury and death linked to that urban space.
breather
LINK “These baboons are even coming into the schools, and some parents are worried that’s it’s only a matter of time before a child gets injured
VO: Belinda Gough’s family has lived peacefully with baboons for the last 60 years. Now she fears for their safety.
Upsound of running inside
VO: While filming, dogs start barking, and 4- year- old Finn reacts with terror
Belinda: He's had he's had some awful experiences where baboon has come right past him into the kitchen and, um, and taken food and that and he's he has nightmares and he wouldn't sleep in his own bed for ages after that
VO: Residents use community alerts to try and stay ahead of the baboons.
Belinda: So normally when you look at your WhatsApp groups and say, okay, let's quickly close up, get the dogs and get the kids in and wait until they've gone past. Um, but it's become so difficult.
VO: We spoke to many young parents off camera, who told us their children are scared to move around their own homes. But they’re worried that speaking out - would see them labeled - as "baboon haters".
“There was some activist standing outside my house and she was screaming from the road while we were traumatised, stuck in our house, and terrified that the baboon would injure one of my children.”
Janice: you don't know who to talk to. You don't know who's filming you.
VO: Sisters Janice and Margaret grew up with baboons, but they’re alarmed by how emboldened they’ve become and shocked at the backlash against complaints.
Janice “You live in the sphere of being labeled and pointed at saying, you're the one that wants the baboons dead and it's not true
VO: Willis says division in the community has deepened since 2022.
Peter …..keyboard warriors were, uh, splitting into those who were fiercely animal rights activist oriented and those who were saying, yes, but I don't want the baboons in my kitchen
Breather
Govan: These baboons are a danger to animals and children, don't you think?
Pauline: No, definitely not.
Govan: But they have mauled animals.
Pauline: They don't maul - baboons do not attack dogs.
Govan: Let me say they have viciously injured animals.
Pauline: No No The baboons do not attack.
Govan: But hey have
Pauline: They defend, they defend. I have been in situations where a dachshund has walked right through a troop of 40 baboons
Govan: For every single thing that you say. You're saying it's the conduct of the other person. It's not the baboons, it's the dog. It's not the baboons. It's the kid. It's not the baboons coming into the house to raid. It's the people who left the doors open. Surely you don't believe that.
Pauline: Look if you bring your children up to really love wildlife, there's lots of children, even in my road, who are not bothered by the baboons. Their parents actually walk them outside to meet the baboons. They love them

Breath/beat
VO: Willis, who’s a professional mediator, has tried to intervene - and build trust. He’s formed a civic coalition - with other concerned citizens.
Peter” We are here to see if we can't develop a really sensible engagement between residents and authorities to get to good outcomes. And for quite a while, they were very welcoming of our voice.
VO: But the progress was short-lived and the stand-off continues. The only thing everyone seems to agree on - is that the baboons are better off in the mountains.
But they differ on how to get them there.
Breather with activist baboon flag waving in the night
We, too, got a taste of the distrust engulfing places like Simon’s Town. While working along the main road as baboons made their way through the town, a group of monitors calming the traffic - took exception to us filming.
“Take your fucking camera out of my face- what are you doing are you one of those sensationalist people”
VO: Perhaps understandably tempers here are frayed, - and many rush to judgement.
Something evident in the widely publicised Kommetjie incident last month.
Upsound of the baboon can't see - you pig how can you hurt an animal
VO: Some onlookers believed this baboon had been pepper-sprayed - as it appeared disorientated. But - it later emerged it had eaten marijuana taken from a house earlier that day
Upsound
VO: In November, the JTT and animal rights groups will face off in court. Accused of failing the animals, one of the biggest complaints leveled against officials is poor waste management. It’s argued that conflict between baboons and local communities - has shown to be reduced when food waste is managed with baboon-proof bins - and collaborative recycling.
But there are no easy answers
Justin “So once baboons have learnt all the tricks that they are learning in urban areas, including breaking windows, removing sliding doors, they. Yeah, you don't unlearn that. “
VO: The JTT declined the interview on the advice of their legal representatives - until after the court case is finalised.
LINK This town has been divided. By baboons! Wild baboons that have been domesticated.

VO: And, in this tension-filled atmosphere - perhaps all - residents, activists and certainly the baboons are victims.

In the absence of resources and guidance from the powers-that-be, residents are left to find solutions - to a population - of habituated baboons

Upsound: And when you catch me, what are you going to do?

I mean, I have never ever felt like that with the baboons before. But it was extremely aggressive, both of them…..” VO: A voice note from a resident of a coastal community outside Cape Town... moments after encountering baboons in her home Margie “ I was screaming and screaming and trying to trying to hit them apart. Michael:. The baboons have a lot of rights. I have no rights at all Belinda “they look at you and they walk straight past you into the kitchen. VO: A longstanding suburban conflict between wild animals - and humans. Peter: there is a very fine line between admiring a baboon, and treating them as though they were your sort of public pets. VO: And - it’s reaching breaking point. Pauline: They are not dangerous breather UPSOUND of Kommetjie conflict people shouting VO: Few issues divide coastal communities more than baboons - as this standoff in Kommetjie, on the Cape Peninsula early last month shows. upsound from standoff VO: About 40 baboons had spent most of the winter sleeping in town - raiding the village in the day - and some residents- had had enough Upsound standoff VO: As their natural habitats shrink, baboons are becoming increasingly habituated in urban spaces across the Peninsula, like Kommetjie and Simonstown. Margie “By this stage the baboon was here passing me , it came through here, Lila was on the chair over there and she spotted it VO: Kommetjie resident Margret Kennedy, has vivid memories of a serious encounter with baboons. She was inside her house at the time - and had left the front door open. A local WhatsApp alert group indicated there were no baboons in the vicinity." Margie “there was just blood everywhere and I ran next door to get Wayne Wayne “The baboon got me in my hand. But then it would go back to Lila and continually, like, shredding her. VO: Baboons had got into her home, and were attacking her dog. The Pitbull lost an eye - and had an ear ripped off… and was later euthanized. Margie: I was told on that day that it was an isolated incident and nothing like that had ever happened before. 00:11:28:05 and I was also blamed for leaving my front door open VO: But it wasn’t isolated - incidents like this have been escalating. In some areas, like central Simonstown, baboons have taken up permanent residence. LINK “Only 25% of the baboons actually go back into the mountains at night which means there are generations and generations of baboon babies that only know city living , they occupy abandoned buildings, they forage, they eat the stuff in the rubbish , they have become part of Simonstown VO: Peter Willis has been living in Simonstown for 31 years. Govan: Have baboons always been a problem here? Peter: No…….In the mid 2000, they started coming down and it was it got pretty bad VO: In 2010 - the City of Cape Town intervened, developing a baboon management and monitoring protocol, and for 10 years, the baboons stayed largely in the mountains Peter “And then we hit Covid and the troops started realizing they could move in places that they hadn't previously. VO: Residents were working from home; some were feeding the baboons. They saw firsthand how the monitors controversially drove the animals out with paintball guns, relocated them, and occasionally euthanized them. It led to accusations of cruelty and ineptitude against City officials, some of whom - had their tyres slashed or were threatened. Respected Behaviour Ecologist, Professor Justin O Riain, wasn’t spared: He and his family were threatened - and his job put at risk. Justin: And that was probably the most difficult lesson I learned was that facts can't beat Facebook. VO: Amid the public mud-slinging, the baboon management program lost funding - and slowly became ineffectual. Justin: I think they should have had the backbone to stand up and say, well, that's your opinion, … we're carrying on like this because it's the right thing to do. It's rational, it's supported by science and communities, and baboons are benefiting VO: In the vacuum, - the baboons moved in. LINK “There are two baboons in this rubbish bin right now ….1.47 this is why the baboons are in such bad shape. …………… they eating out of rubbish bins and when they cant find anything here, they go into people’s homes Breather Polly Clip “. This was locked. Unfortunately, those two bottom ones weren't. And .. She took out the whole of this window VO: Polly Saul lives alone - and no longer sits outside in her garden. Polly” I was shocked and shattered because everything was closed and locked., and a avo rolled across the counter. So it leapt to follow the other, and I think it thought assumed I was going to take its purchase, and it just leaned over to make sure I didn't. And I think in the process it caught my hand, VO: Baboons carry many diseases, and leave behind huge amounts of faeces. Polly needed a tetanus shot. Polly Clip “And their skills are improving massively and we are helpless. VO: Baboons are actively breaking in - chewing through wooden window frames and breaking burglar bars and trapping dogs inside homes. Breath/beat VO: In August, filmmaker, Micheal Donnely, returned to a house turned upside down by 16 baboons. Michael “I come upstairs and at this stage I have no idea how these guys have got in… there is poos all over the steps all over the walls and everywhere here “They got in here and broke the latch Govan “All this gear, did the gear get damaged A lot- there was a camera that they poop in, they threw it out the window, there a 35 mm lens and 1.2 and I have no idea where it is “I think we are looking at R250 000 maybe R300 000 seriously Michael:. The baboons have a lot of rights. I feel that I have no rights in this thing that nobody's listening to what is happening here? Everyone is pretending it's a sort of a non-event VO: Since June 2022 SANParks, Cape Nature, and the City, collectively called the JTT, have been formulating an urban baboon strategic management plan. But the process has been marred by political infighting and budget disagreements. Now - the City has terminated what’s left of the existing baboon monitoring program. Breather LINK “Residents feel the authorities are missing in action and their desperate pleas for help disappear into the void VO: Animal activists like Pauline Suddards - are trying to fill the gap. Pauline: when the baboons move across the road. And then I have a flag just to warn traffic because the baboons' fur is the same colour as the tarmac. And to also keep them safe so that nobody interferes with them before they go to roost. Govan: Is that a self-appointed function? Pauline: Um, when you say self-appointed, if I'm there doing traffic control, um, I just make sure that they, you know, they stay away from danger really VO: Like many in these areas, Pauline believes people who choose to live here - should adapt to the baboons. Pauline: You know, you need to embrace what comes with Kommetjie. All the wildlife, the otters, the baboons, everything that's here. Justin: I think suggesting to people that they should learn to live with baboons in a suburb is is a very bad idea. And our data is clear on this, that if baboons spend time in urban areas, they will suffer from all manner of injury and death linked to that urban space. breather LINK “These baboons are even coming into the schools, and some parents are worried that’s it’s only a matter of time before a child gets injured VO: Belinda Gough’s family has lived peacefully with baboons for the last 60 years. Now she fears for their safety. Upsound of running inside VO: While filming, dogs start barking, and 4- year- old Finn reacts with terror Belinda: He's had he's had some awful experiences where baboon has come right past him into the kitchen and, um, and taken food and that and he's he has nightmares and he wouldn't sleep in his own bed for ages after that VO: Residents use community alerts to try and stay ahead of the baboons. Belinda: So normally when you look at your WhatsApp groups and say, okay, let's quickly close up, get the dogs and get the kids in and wait until they've gone past. Um, but it's become so difficult. VO: We spoke to many young parents off camera, who told us their children are scared to move around their own homes. But they’re worried that speaking out - would see them labeled - as "baboon haters". “There was some activist standing outside my house and she was screaming from the road while we were traumatised, stuck in our house, and terrified that the baboon would injure one of my children.” Janice: you don't know who to talk to. You don't know who's filming you. VO: Sisters Janice and Margaret grew up with baboons, but they’re alarmed by how emboldened they’ve become and shocked at the backlash against complaints. Janice “You live in the sphere of being labeled and pointed at saying, you're the one that wants the baboons dead and it's not true VO: Willis says division in the community has deepened since 2022. Peter …..keyboard warriors were, uh, splitting into those who were fiercely animal rights activist oriented and those who were saying, yes, but I don't want the baboons in my kitchen Breather Govan: These baboons are a danger to animals and children, don't you think? Pauline: No, definitely not. Govan: But they have mauled animals. Pauline: They don't maul - baboons do not attack dogs. Govan: Let me say they have viciously injured animals. Pauline: No No The baboons do not attack. Govan: But hey have Pauline: They defend, they defend. I have been in situations where a dachshund has walked right through a troop of 40 baboons Govan: For every single thing that you say. You're saying it's the conduct of the other person. It's not the baboons, it's the dog. It's not the baboons. It's the kid. It's not the baboons coming into the house to raid. It's the people who left the doors open. Surely you don't believe that. Pauline: Look if you bring your children up to really love wildlife, there's lots of children, even in my road, who are not bothered by the baboons. Their parents actually walk them outside to meet the baboons. They love them Breath/beat VO: Willis, who’s a professional mediator, has tried to intervene - and build trust. He’s formed a civic coalition - with other concerned citizens. Peter” We are here to see if we can't develop a really sensible engagement between residents and authorities to get to good outcomes. And for quite a while, they were very welcoming of our voice. VO: But the progress was short-lived and the stand-off continues. The only thing everyone seems to agree on - is that the baboons are better off in the mountains. But they differ on how to get them there. Breather with activist baboon flag waving in the night We, too, got a taste of the distrust engulfing places like Simon’s Town. While working along the main road as baboons made their way through the town, a group of monitors calming the traffic - took exception to us filming. “Take your fucking camera out of my face- what are you doing are you one of those sensationalist people” VO: Perhaps understandably tempers here are frayed, - and many rush to judgement. Something evident in the widely publicised Kommetjie incident last month. Upsound of the baboon can't see - you pig how can you hurt an animal VO: Some onlookers believed this baboon had been pepper-sprayed - as it appeared disorientated. But - it later emerged it had eaten marijuana taken from a house earlier that day Upsound VO: In November, the JTT and animal rights groups will face off in court. Accused of failing the animals, one of the biggest complaints leveled against officials is poor waste management. It’s argued that conflict between baboons and local communities - has shown to be reduced when food waste is managed with baboon-proof bins - and collaborative recycling. But there are no easy answers Justin “So once baboons have learnt all the tricks that they are learning in urban areas, including breaking windows, removing sliding doors, they. Yeah, you don't unlearn that. “ VO: The JTT declined the interview on the advice of their legal representatives - until after the court case is finalised. LINK This town has been divided. By baboons! Wild baboons that have been domesticated. VO: And, in this tension-filled atmosphere - perhaps all - residents, activists and certainly the baboons are victims. In the absence of resources and guidance from the powers-that-be, residents are left to find solutions - to a population - of habituated baboons Upsound: And when you catch me, what are you going to do?

metadata.Unique Selling Point: There baboons have literally moved into town, taking over, and nobody is taking responsibility and the level of trauma of residents is falling on deaf ears, never mind the level of damage to property. A few statistics from Kommetjie - 55% of residents have DAILY encounters with baboons; 70% have had damage to their property; 85% have had baboons in their homes; 35% keep their windows permanently closed; and 11 % have had to have pets euthanased. Baboons are holding residents hostage in their own homes in Kommetjie and Simon’s Town. They are no longer afraid of people. They used to be frightened of men but they have become so habituated that if confronted they just bare their teeth and rise up in attack stance. Children are so traumatised that they won’t play in their own gardens. They are not safe at home or school. The baboons recently walked into a preschool and grabbed the food from the hands of a terrified 3-year-old, a carefree confident child now clings to her mother’s legs. A large male baboon slipped into a home and entered the bedroom where a dog was asleep. The startled dog awoke and was ripped apart. Its eye torn out, ear ripped off and scalped. The vet had no alternative but to euthanase it. A dog let out to relieve itself in the rain after its owner had checked the baboon alert group was attacked so badly, it also had to be euthanased. A child with severe autism’s companion labrador came between a child and a baboon when it entered their home; both child and dog are now severely traumatised
metadata.Summary: For the last 3 years, the once internationally recognised urban wildlife baboon management programme has broken down after a massive social media campaign waged by baboon activists after the Kataza saga. The situation came to a head in Kommetjie last Sunday when residents held a peaceful protest outside a burned-out building in the main street of Kommetjie. The baboons come down from the mountain every night and are escorted into town by a self-appointed baboon monitor, Briton Pauline Sudders. Her concern is that they don’t get run over - but she doesn’t stop there. She shouts at children skateboarding that they must keep quiet because the baboons want to sleep and confronts people carrying any kind of defence against being attacked. Matters have been brewing since the Kataza saga 3 years ago where residents protested the relocation of a male baboon from Kommetjie to Constantia, which the baboon activists saw as him being removed from his family. Activist Jenni Trethowan escorted him back over the mountain, but on hisd return, Kataza rejected his so-called “family” and headed out again. He was relocated to Limpopo amid a media storm, and later released into an area where farmers boast of having shot over 200 baboons – there is a good chance Kataza has also been shot. Kataza was a turning point for the City of Cape Town because the social media backlash was so extreme. This activist media campaign called on international tourists to boycott Cape Town because “we kill baboons”. The city could ill afford to lose any more tourism after the Covid-19 pandemic. Internationally recognised wildlife academic and baboon specialist, Dr Justin O Riain, was labelled “Dr Death” and a deep fake video circulated of him “doing vivisections”. Complaints were lodged on a daily basis to his employers, UCT. He was investigated numerous times and eventually asked to stop his research because the media campaign was so vicious. It nearly ended his career. He received repeat death threats to both himself and his family. The City stopped implementing the scientific protocols on how to deal with wildlife on the urban edge - a world-recognised programme that had worked for over 10 years. Fake science and the emotive media campaign were too much for the authorities. Now when residents are being attacked in their own homes, the baboon activists stand outside and say “I am filming you - don’t hurt the baboons”, and offer no help. This is a voice note from a mother whose entire week’s food was destroyed, her 10-year-old trapped under the stairs. For three days running, the same baboon attacked her home. One evening her 6 foot tall, 19-year-old champion windsurfer son tried to hold the door closed in the face of an aggressive male baboon - he lost the tussle and the baboon got in, trapping them in the bedroom. People fear defending themselves because their activist neighbours threaten to burn their homes down The three responsible authorities - SANparks, CapeNature and the City of Cape Town - have for decades tossed this hot potato back and forth, all claiming they either don’t have jurisdiction or funding. Finally, in 2023 then Environment Minister Barbara Creecey interceded and appointed a Joint task Team. SANParks agreed to put R8-million into strategic electrified baboon fences. CapeNature put in R2-million but don’t have budget for operational costs; and the COCT are cancelling the rangers’ contract at the end of September. The fences are useless without rangers.
